subject: Anthropology
title: Ranked Societies
description: A quick win: understand Ranked Societies.

hook.text: Everyone has a place. Chiefs sit higher, commoners sit lower. Rank is inherited, and moving up is nearly impossible.

buildup.text: Ranked societies give unequal prestige to lineages but limit access to wealth less strictly than stratified ones.

discovery.text: Polynesian chiefdoms are classic examples. Birth order and genealogy determine your rank in the social hierarchy.

twist.text: High rank brings duties, not just privileges. Chiefs must redistribute wealth or lose respect and legitimacy.

climax.text: Ranked societies sit between equality and stratification. Prestige is unequal, but extreme wealth gaps are limited.

punchline.text: Rank exists, but hoarding is still forbidden.

quiz.question: What distinguishes ranked from egalitarian societies?
options: Lineages have unequal prestige but extreme wealth gaps are limited
Everyone is completely equal in ranked societies

details.summary: Ranked societies assign different prestige levels to kin groups but without corresponding differences in wealth or power. High-ranking families hold ceremonial authority while economic resources remain relatively equally distributed across the community.
details.whyItMatters: Ranked societies occupy a middle ground between egalitarian and stratified systems. They show how prestige hierarchies can exist without economic inequality, challenging the assumption that status and wealth always go together.
takeaways: Ranked societies have prestige hierarchies without economic inequality
High-ranking families hold ceremonial rather than economic power
They represent a transitional form between egalitarian and stratified systems

faq.question: How do ranked societies differ from stratified ones?
faq.answer: In ranked societies, high status brings prestige and ceremonial authority but not disproportionate wealth. In stratified societies, high status brings wealth, power, and prestige together. Pacific Northwest Coast chiefdoms are classic examples of ranked societies.

faq.question: What role does kinship play in ranked societies?
faq.answer: Rank is typically inherited through birth order and lineage. The firstborn of the firstborn may hold the highest rank. Junior lineages hold lower prestige. Kinship determines one's position in the prestige hierarchy, making genealogy politically significant.
